items.stem: A product sponsor asks that the pass threshold for a new support-ticket deflection feature be 'calibrated once we see baseline numbers' from the first week in production, with a board review scheduled before wider rollout. What should the evaluation team do?

opts.t: Calibrate the pass threshold after the first week of production data, then lock it before the board review.
Re-anchor the threshold to a small non-zero rate, since this is an open-ended, model-judged property.
Track the deflection rate for two weeks without setting any threshold, then bring the raw numbers to the board.
Reject the proposal and set the threshold now, anchored to the success criterion or the process it replaces.

items.whyRight: The stakeholder is asking for the same trap the section warns against: a bar set after the numbers land only describes the result. The team should set the threshold now, anchored to the success criterion or the process it replaces, and log any later change as a deliberate revision.

whyWrong.A: Setting the bar after the first week of data is the deferred-calibration request restated with a deadline; a post-hoc bar only ever gets revised downward once inconvenient.
whyWrong.B: No open-ended 0% bar was proposed here; the actual ask is about timing, not the numeric value, so re-anchoring to a small non-zero rate answers a question nobody raised.
whyWrong.C: Tracking the rate without ever setting a threshold discards the requirement outright; a finished metric needs a named failure, denominator, segment, and threshold agreed before results arrive.

items.t1Clause: be 'calibrated once we see baseline numbers' from the first week in production
items.factAnswerRaw: Reject — set it now, revise it as a recorded decision later

items.stem: An assistant's 500-case evaluation set reports 96% accuracy, yet the support team logs steady customer complaints. Ahead of the quarterly review, an engineer proposes expanding the same set to 2,000 cases collected the same way. What should the team do?

opts.t: Approve the expansion — 2,000 cases collected the same way will look more defensible at the review.
Generate the extra cases with the same model that serves production, to hold down labeling costs.
Cut the set to the 40 most recently hand-verified cases and present those as the new baseline.
Reject the expansion — the same sampling process at four times the scale still narrows around a wrong number.

items.whyRight: Nothing about scale fixes a set that already omits the failure classes customers are hitting. Four times the cases collected the same way produces four times the bias and a tighter, still-wrong interval — the defect is composition, and only rebuilding from real production failures addresses it.

whyWrong.A: More cases collected by the same process only tighten the interval around the same biased number; the set's composition, not its count, is why complaints keep coming.
whyWrong.B: The serving model's own competence and phrasing distribution become the ground truth, guaranteeing the added cases contain nothing the model cannot already handle.
whyWrong.C: This set's problem is missing failure coverage, not unverified labels; cutting to 40 cases here throws away the little signal the set already has.

items.t1Clause: 500-case evaluation set reports 96% accuracy, yet the support team logs steady customer complaints

items.stem: A team runs a controlled A/B test on a prompt change and sits at day 4 of a planned 14-day run. The primary metric already looks favourable, but the variant breached the declared p95 latency guardrail. Select the two required actions.

opts.t: Continue the test through its full declared 14-day duration instead of stopping early on the favourable read.
Do not ship, because one high-value segment regressed twelve points while the aggregate metric improved.
Extend the run past its declared 14-day duration until the latency guardrail is no longer breached, then ship.
Do not ship the variant, since it breached the p95 latency guardrail declared before the test began.

items.whyRight: The test is only four days into a planned fourteen, so a favourable early read must not stop it — the stopping rule runs to the declared duration regardless of interim numbers. Guardrails only block: a breached latency guardrail forces no-ship no matter what the primary metric shows.

whyWrong.B: No segment data of any kind appears in this run; the twelve-point regression is real for a different situation in this section, but nothing here supports invoking it.
whyWrong.C: Extending the run past its declared length does not undo a guardrail breach, and guardrails exist precisely to block shipment regardless of how much longer the test runs.

items.t1Clause: the variant breached the p95 latency guardrail declared before the test began

items.stem: A support assistant answers accurately across most document types but is reliably wrong on scanned PDF contracts, while performing well on the rest of the corpus. A director proposes upgrading to a larger, three-times-costlier model. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Move to the larger, three-times-costlier model, since a broad accuracy failure usually signals insufficient model capability.
Check how the scanned PDF contracts are parsed, chunked, and indexed compared with the rest of the corpus.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the assistant to answer scanned contracts more carefully.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating the correct answer format for every document type in the corpus.

items.whyRight: The failure is confined to one document type while the rest of the corpus is answered correctly, which points at how that specific type is parsed, chunked, and indexed — not at a general capability gap the model carries everywhere.

whyWrong.A: The failure is narrow, confined to one document type, not the broad multi-step reasoning breakdown a genuine model-capability gap produces; the costlier model was never implicated.
whyWrong.C: An instruction to be more careful cannot recover content that was never correctly parsed or indexed in the first place; it patches downstream of the actual fault.
whyWrong.D: Nothing here describes inconsistent formatting across runs; the stated symptom is being wrong on one document type, which few-shot formatting examples do not address.

items.t1Clause: reliably wrong on scanned PDF contracts, while performing well on the rest of the corpus

items.stem: A compliance-mandated policy preamble is sent unchanged on every request to a customer assistant, and both p95 latency and the monthly token bill are over target. The preamble cannot be shortened without legal sign-off. What should the team do?

opts.t: Truncate the preamble to the sections used most often and pursue legal sign-off for the cut afterward.
Reorder the request so the static preamble comes first and enable prompt caching on that stable prefix.
Enable response streaming so the answer appears sooner and the latency figures come down.
Summarize the preamble with an extra model call at request time to shorten what gets sent.

items.whyRight: The preamble is identical on every request, so caching that stable prefix reuses it at a fraction of the cost and latency without dropping a single mandated word. Ordering static content first is what makes the prefix cacheable at all.

whyWrong.A: Cutting compliance-mandated language is a regression the requirement forbids, not a saving, and pursuing sign-off after the cut has already shipped inverts the actual approval order.
whyWrong.C: Streaming only changes when tokens appear on screen; it does not reduce total completion time or the token bill the stem says is over target.
whyWrong.D: Summarizing at request time adds a full extra model invocation with its own cost and latency, and risks degrading the precision of mandated policy language.

items.t1Clause: The preamble cannot be shortened without legal sign-off
items.factAnswerRaw: Order static content first and enable prompt caching

notes: g34: built from two independently-true rows of 4.9's decision table per dispatch instruction — F-4.9-04 (stopping rule: run to declared duration) for A, and F-4.9-05 (guardrail breach blocks shipment) for D. This is a different row-pair than Paper 2's g36 (which combined F-4.9-03 randomization-unit + F-4.9-06 segment-masking), so no content overlap with the prior paper's multi-item on this section.

g34: shape S3 ('recent change is the cause vs coincidence, pinned variables point elsewhere') is a loose fit for 4.9's release-path content — applied here as 'the early favourable read may be coincidental noise, and the variable that actually decides shipment is the guardrail, not the metric.' Flagging as a soft substitution candidate rather than swapping outright, since the multi-select shape doesn't map cleanly onto any single S-archetype's binary framing.

g35-D and g36-C use EVIDENCE-MISMATCH and WRONG-AXIS respectively per the brief's request to diversify beyond HALF-MOVE/WRONG-AXIS; several other distractors (g32-A ARCHITECTED, g33-A HALF-MOVE, g33-B DISCARD, g35-A DISCARD, g36-A DISCARD, g36-C WRONG-AXIS) were deliberately kept aligned with this corpus's own literal family labels in its exam-scenario blocks for grounding fidelity — no DETECTIVE-FOR-PREVENTIVE was used anywhere in this batch, since D4's evaluation/testing/optimization content (metrics, datasets, A/B tests, diagnosis, cost/latency) doesn't naturally present a capability-removal-vs-monitoring choice; that family fits D3/D5/D7 tool-scoping content per the brief, not D4.

All five items' T1/T2/T3/T4 checks were verified against real rows in the cited sections before shipping — none are flagged as IRREDUCIBLE. t1Alt letters all resolve to nameable rows: g32->B (F-4.1-04), g33->C (F-4.3-03), g34->B (F-4.9-06), g35->A (F-4.10-07), g36->A (F-4.11-02's converse: cutting non-required sections).
